description: Agreement between the Swift app's language decision (NLLanguageRecognizer under the gates of language.json) and the Rust core's (whatlang, restricted to the languages NLLanguageRecognizer can answer, under the same gates with the confidence gate re-tuned to above 0.59 for whatlang's scale, HK-421), on natural sentences of the kind replies hold (spec #100 slice 2.5, ticket #160; ADR 0011: the speech text rules are shared, the engines and voices are per OS). expected.swift is the decision the Swift app made (a language code, or null for undecided, read as English). A Rust decision that differs is either resolved toward the Swift one or recorded as an accepted difference: expected gains "core" with the core's decision, the reason says why the difference is accepted, and the ledger names it. Two kinds are accepted: the core undecided, so the reply reads in English (HK-421), and Han-only text the Swift app read as Japanese reading as Chinese (HK-420). The corpus covers en, de, fr, es, it, pt, nl, simplified and traditional Chinese, ja, ko, mixed CJK and Latin, short strings, Han-only text, text that is no language, and code-heavy prose.
function: speech::dominant_language (Swift: CoreBridge.dominantLanguage(of:); until slice 2.5 TTSService.dominantLanguageCode(of:)) — input the text, expected {swift} (plus core for an accepted difference), each a language code or null
verifiedBy: DESIGN.md v1.2 A, v2.14; Tests/PowerUpTests/SpeechFixtureTests.swift testLanguageAgreementTable plays it through CoreBridge.dominantLanguage(of:) and compares expected.core where the table records an accepted difference, expected.swift everywhere else. Rust: rust/powerup-core/tests/speech.rs language_agreement_cases runs speech::dominant_language and compares expected.core where the table records an accepted difference, expected.swift everywhere else.
capturedAgainst: Swift 5.9.2 Foundation and NaturalLanguage (Xcode 15.2) on macOS 27.2, PowerUp at 67659a4

cases.name: han: 東京駅
cases.input: 東京駅
cases.reason: Han-only text: a recognizer answer of zh, ja or ko is trusted whatever its confidence, so Han with no kana can still read as ja (HK-212). Swift: NLLanguageRecognizer says Japanese at 1.00 with 3 letters; its CJK answer is trusted. Accepted difference (HK-420): the core's whatlang decides Han-only text by its script, zh with no kana, and has no lexicon that knows Japanese words written in kanji; a Japanese reply holds kana, which decide ja in both.
